briefs.competency: use diagrams and illustrations to describe the arrangement, spacing, and relative motion of the particles in each of the three states (phases) of matter
existing_facts_en: When a gas is put under pressure by reducing the volume of its container, the space between particles is reduced and the gas is compressed.
Tiny particles (atoms and molecules) make up all matter and never stop moving! Solids: packed tight, just vibrating. Liquids: close but sliding. Gases: far apart and zooming fast!

Why are solids so firm?

In a solid, tiny particles are packed close together and barely move, keeping it firm!
You can't just squeeze a solid smaller! Its particles are already packed tight with almost no gaps. That's why solids keep the same volume—they can't be squished down!

Why does sound travel faster in steel than in air?

Sound travels about fifteen times faster in steel! Particles in solids are packed closer together, so they pass vibrations more quickly.
Why are solids so firm?  In a solid, tiny particles are packed close together and barely move, keeping it firm!
Why does sound travel faster in steel than in air?  Sound travels about fifteen times faster in steel! Particles in solids are packed closer together, so they pass vibrations more quickly.
When a solid melts, heat makes its particles vibrate faster! They vibrate so much that they finally break free from their fixed positions.
Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid! Some particles gain enough energy to break free and escape right into the air.
In a gas, particles are super spread out! They are about ten times farther apart from each other than in a liquid or solid.
Even in ice, particles still vibrate in place! The cold does not completely stop their tiny, wiggly motion.
A solid has a fixed shape and volume. A liquid has fixed volume but takes the container's shape, and a gas takes both!
What causes gas pressure inside a container?  Countless tiny particles zoom around and hit the container walls! Each tiny collision gives a small push, and together they create gas pressure.

Why do solids, liquids, and gases behave so differently?  It's all about forces! Strong forces lock solid particles in place, weaker ones let liquid particles slide, and gas particles have almost no pull between them.
Liquid particles slide past each other, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
Most of a gas is empty space, because its particles are spread so far apart that they barely bump into each other.
When a solid melts, heat makes its particles vibrate faster until they break free from their fixed positions.
Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid when some particles gain enough energy to escape into the air.
In a solid, particles are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern, while in liquids and gases the arrangement is random.
Water boils at about 100 degrees Celsius, when liquid particles throughout the water gain enough energy to form bubbles of gas.
Condensation is when gas particles lose energy, slow down, and stick together to form a liquid, like drops on a cold glass.
Freezing happens when a liquid cools and its particles slow down enough to lock into fixed positions, forming a solid.
Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide that turns directly into gas without melting, a process called sublimation.
Frost on leaves forms when water vapor in the air turns directly into ice without becoming liquid first.
Gas particles have the most energy, liquid particles have less, and solid particles have the least energy of all.
In a gas, particles are about ten times farther apart from each other than in a liquid or solid.
Even in ice, particles still vibrate in place, so cold does not completely stop their motion.
A drop of food coloring spreads through water because moving liquid particles bump into the color and carry it around.
The smell of cooking adobo spreads through the house because gas particles from the food move and mix with the air.
A solid has a fixed shape and volume, a liquid has fixed volume but takes the container's shape, and a gas takes both.
Gas particles move in straight lines until they collide with each other or with the walls of their container.
Ice floats on water because water particles arrange in a more open pattern when frozen, making ice less dense.
When PAGASA reports rain, water vapor in clouds condenses into droplets that grow heavy enough to fall.
Hot lava from Mayon volcano cools and solidifies into rock as its particles slow down and lock into place.
Gas pressure comes from countless tiny particles hitting the inside walls of a container, each collision giving a small push.
When a substance is heated, its particles gain energy and move faster; when cooled, they slow down and move closer together.
Strong forces hold solid particles in fixed positions, weaker forces allow liquid particles to slide, and gas particles have almost no forces pulling them together.
Most substances expand when heated because their particles move faster and spread farther apart, taking up more space.
